tn_hanger_the.blurb: A steep, bolted wall in the Little Clear Creek section of the Obed country, on the Cumberland Plateau. The rock is hard sandstone, and the routes run along a ledge about thirty feet up the face, with a bolted cable on the awkward stretches of that ledge. The climbing is almost all sport, with one aid line, and it is hard by Obed standards: most lines sit in the 5.12 range, backed by a few 5.11s and a handful of 5.13s, so it suits strong climbers rather than beginners. Expect overhanging, powerful movement and bring a stick clip, since first bolts in the Obed tend to be high.

tn_orchard_the.blurb: A sector of the limestone cliff above the Cumberland River in Clarksville. The Orchard is almost entirely sport climbing, with a single trad line, and it is one of the friendlier stretches of the cliff: the bulk of the routes fall between 5.8 and 5.10, with a few easier ones and some 5.11s on top. Expect small edges, pockets and flexing flakes, with routes in the 35 to 70 foot range. Leaf cover gives shade in summer, and the cliff takes direct sun through winter. It is usually quiet, and the walk from the parking area is short.

tn_lower_middle_creek.blurb: The lower section of Middle Creek, a bouldering area on Suck Creek Road northwest of Chattanooga. Boulders are scattered through the woods beside a creek with good swimming holes. The problems are demanding: nothing here is an easy warm-up, grades run from V2 up to V10, and most land between V5 and V8, so it is a spot for climbers already comfortable on harder boulders. Several boulders stay damp through summer, so cooler months are the better bet.
tn_lower_middle_creek.parking_note: Pull off along Suck Creek Road at the construction barriers, roughly seven tenths of a mile beyond River Drifters when you are driving out from Chattanooga.

tn_fort_sandstone.blurb: A sport-only section of the Obed on the Cumberland Plateau, set on hard sandstone. Unlike the steep roofs the Obed is best known for, much of the climbing here is vertical and slabby, with some steeper lines mixed in. Most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12, but there is also a small cluster of 5.7 to 5.9 routes that suit newer leaders. It sits deep along the cliffline trails, so expect a longer walk than at the road-side walls.
tn_fort_sandstone.approach: A fairly long walk along the cliffline trails beyond the Tierrany Roofs and the Middle Obed section. A fainter path drops to a lower trail past Slammer Ledge, where a big wooden ladder climbs to the ledge. The upper trail fades out, so stay on the lower one.

tn_buzzard_point.blurb: A cliff on a large point that splits the gorge in Laurel-Snow, on the Cumberland Plateau near Dayton. The rock is good and the buttress catches sun for most of the day, which makes it a fall and winter crag; summer afternoons bring fast storms. It is a mix of sport and some spicy trad, much of it in an old-school style. The grades lean hard: most routes are 5.11 or 5.12, with a smaller number of 5.10s, a couple of 5.8s and a few 5.13s, so it is a place for experienced leaders.
tn_buzzard_point.parking_note: Leave Dayton on Delaware Avenue and go a little over a mile past the Highway 30 junction. A gravel road branches off toward the Laurel-Snow sign and ends at the lot where the trail starts.

tn_space_odyssey_shotgun_area.blurb: A tight group of sandstone boulders inside the Stone Fort bouldering at Little Rock City near Chattanooga. The boulders form a small alcove with a corridor behind it, and the area is known for a pair of tall, blunt arete lines a few feet apart. Problems run from V0 to V12, but the bulk are V1 to V7, so there is something for most climbers if you are happy with tall, committing moves. Bring plenty of pads.
tn_space_odyssey_shotgun_area.parking_note: Leave your vehicle in the climber spots near the clubhouse of the Montlake golf course, off Brow Lake Road in Soddy-Daisy.

tn_fairway_boulders.blurb: A long line of sandstone boulders at Stone Fort, strung out for hundreds of yards along a forest edge beside the fairway grass near Chattanooga. The rock quality is excellent, and the problems are varied. Grades run from V2 to V10, with the weight in the V3 to V5 range, so there are plenty of moderate problems alongside a few harder ones. The setting is open, and it is easy to walk from one boulder to the next.

tn_devil_s_race_track.blurb: Two rock fins that jut from the mountainside beside the interstate at Caryville, close to Cove Lake. The rock is solid, though moss is a problem in places. Routes are a mix of sport and trad, spread over a tall north wall, a south face and a lower wall. Grades range from 5.6 to 5.12, with most routes between 5.8 and 5.11. Bolts and anchors are well placed. Expect traffic noise, and the trail is steep in places and slippery when wet.
tn_devil_s_race_track.approach: Hike up alongside the creek, cross where it divides, and follow cairns up the gully to reach the lower wall. The north face is the first big section you meet, and the wall gets shorter as you continue uphill.

tn_6_the_amphitheater.blurb: A section of the Tennessee Wall, a hard sandstone crag above the Tennessee River gorge near Chattanooga. Most routes here are trad, with a smaller group of sport lines. The grades lean demanding: about a third are 5.11, and there are a good number of 5.12s and 5.13s, plus a few easier routes in the 5.5 to 5.10 range. The Tennessee Wall faces south and takes full sun, so it is a prime cold-season crag and gets very hot in summer.
tn_6_the_amphitheater.parking_note: Take River Canyon Road out of Chattanooga to the lot at the campsite turn-off for the wall. Keep vehicles off the road.
